analysis.one_liner: Lets states regulate towing done without the car owner's consent.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let states crack down on predatory towing, died in a House subcommittee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal law, states can regulate only the price a towing company charges when it tows your car without your permission—everything else about how that tow is done is shielded by federal preemption. This bill would strike those limits so states could write their own rules covering the whole tow truck operation, from when a car can be towed to how the business is run. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers whose parked or disabled cars get towed without their consent. The bill would give state governments power to set rules for those tows—something federal law currently limits to pricing—so states could require notice, receipts, fair procedures, and curbs on aggressive towing practices.

how_it_helps.text: Today federal law lets states regulate only the price of non-consensual towing; the bill would let states regulate the operations themselves, including when and how a car can be towed without the owner's consent.

Non-consensual towing—towing a car without the owner's permission—is the practice the bill's title calls predatory, and it mostly affects parked drivers and accident victims who have no say in choosing a towing company.

analysis.who_pays: Towing companies, especially those profiting from towing cars without the owner's consent, who would lose their federal shield from state regulation and face new state rules and enforcement.

drawbacks.text: Federal preemption of interstate trucking regulation exists partly so that carriers moving across state lines face one set of national rules rather than 50 conflicting ones; loosening it for towing could create a patchwork of state requirements for towing companies operating across borders.
The bill gives states broad power to regulate all tow truck operations, which could impose compliance costs on small towing businesses beyond the predatory practices it targets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—letting states stop predatory towing practices that can cost drivers hundreds of dollars and their vehicles—outweighs the cost, which is mainly a modest compliance burden on towing companies and some risk of a patchwork of state rules for interstate carriers. But the bill never advanced far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested or debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's Highways and Transit Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without any hearing, vote, or further action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 21, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, and no further action was ever taken.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill would amend federal law so states could regulate tow truck operations performed without the owner's consent, rather than only the price of such towing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Towing companies keep the federal shield from state regulation that lets predatory towing practices continue unchecked.

for.name: Rep. James P. Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee / Highways and Transit Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Highways and Transit Subcommittee, where it was never taken up.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member acted on the bill and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would strip towing operators of the federal preemption that currently shields most of their work from state regulation, exposing them to state rules on when and how they can tow a car without the owner's consent. Ordinary drivers would gain protection from surprise tows and fees.
